title: VPC upgrade sequencing, Murphy tests, and TF module proofs
content:
Purpose
This doc captures an experimental upgrade sequencing approach and a set of lightweight "Murphy" tests (failure simulations) we want to run during customer VPC / on-prem package upgrades. It also contains short Terraform module "proof" snippets and operational checklists we can hand to SEs for staging. Goal is to reduce surprise on the cutover day and provide an observable gating mechanism so we can abort early.

Context / why this is different
- We keep getting non-deterministic regressions in middle-of-night upgrades when customers have custom routing/egress proxies and older BMCs.
- Existing playbooks cover high-level runbooks; this is targeted at the sequence and the telemetry gates (what to watch, in what order, and simple fault-injection tests).
- Intended audience: SE, SRE on-call for upgrade, and the customer networking lead.

Scope
In scope: VPC network configuration changes that accompany Redwood Private upgrades (eg, service endpoints, egress rules, NAT updates, new sidecar ranges), Terraform module version bumps and migration steps for tfstate, and observable gating for canary waves.
Out of scope: application-level migrations inside customer tenants, PKI/key rotations handled by KMS team (we'll link to their runbook).

High-level sequencing (safe-by-default ordering)
1) Pre-checks (non-impacting) - run from SE laptop or via a staging CI job:
   - TF plan against a read-only mock state (see snippet below)
   - Verify control-plane endpoint connectivity (controlplane.redwood.internal -> customer VPC)
   - Validate routing table references still resolve and there are no overlapping CIDR deltas
   - Snapshot current tfstate (s3/gcs) + export vault refs used by module

2) Dry apply to staging tenant in the customer's VPC (no public traffic) - quick smoke:
   - Apply modules that only add resources (security groups, Cloud Router rules)
   - Run health-check probes from internal canary agent to all egress targets

3) Canary wave (1–2 hosts) - real traffic but constrained:
   - Apply modules that change path-based routing or introduce service proxies
   - Start with 1 host behind a canary route; enable verbose telemetry (trace + logs)
   - Run Murphy tests (below) after stabilization window (5–10m)

4) Broad rollout (50%–100%)
   - If canary passes, proceed to batched apply across remaining hosts with pause points and automated rollback on failing telemetry gates

Murphy tests (failure simulations)
- Purpose: lightweight, deterministic checks to reveal common post-upgrade failures before broad rollout. Each test must be reversible quickly.
- Test A: DNAT/egress block simulation
  - Temporarily inject a deny rule for one egress IP range for the canary host; verify proper fallback (Redwood runtime fallback to alternate egress) and no token leakage. Expected: 502 logged for the canary request only, fallback succeeded.
- Test B: Latency spike injection
  - Insert an artificial 200–500ms delay on the egress proxy for canary host; verify SLO alert triggers and autoscaler doesn't overreact. Expected: metric spike + no scale crash.
- Test C: Partial KV cache miss storm
  - Clear subset of model KV cache on canary host; ensure token rate and latency remain within tolerances; observe cache warm-up pattern.
- Test D: TF state conflict simulation
  - Simulate stale lock by creating a fake lock entry (in staging bucket) and ensure operator-facing tooling fails fast and provides deterministic remediation.

Telemetry gating (what to watch, thresholds)
- Pre-rollout baseline collection window: 30m for latency, 1h for error rates and token throughput.
- Immediate canary gates (5–10m windows):
  - 95p latency increase > 15% over baseline -> hold/rollback
  - Error rate (4xx/5xx) > 0.5% absolute bump -> hold/rollback
  - Token cost delta > 12% for same workload (indicates degenerate batching) -> investigate
- Post-mortem gates: CRITICAL on any data-exfil patterns in egress logs (trigger sec-team page)

Terraform module proofs (short snippets + rationale)
- Goal: tiny, auditable snippets we can run during pre-check to ensure our modules behave under partial-state conditions. Keep them minimal; avoid touching production resources.

Snippet 1: plan-only check against a copy of tfstate (example pseudocode):

  // run in CI job (bash)
  export TF_VAR_customer_prefix="cust-ACME"
  cp s3://redwood-tfstates/cust-acme.tfstate /tmp/cust-acme.tfstate.copy
  terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-tfstates" -reconfigure
  terraform plan -state=/tmp/cust-acme.tfstate.copy -out=/tmp/plan.out || (echo "plan failed" && exit 1)
  terraform show -json /tmp/plan.out | jq '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions != ["no-op"])' > /tmp/changes.json

Notes: we use a copied state so we don't inadvertently take locks. The operator should verify no destructive changes in plan before proceeding.

Snippet 2: state-parity check for module inputs

  // small go/python script (conceptual)
  // verify that the module inputs (cidr ranges, route table ids) in TF vars match the audited tags on cloud resources
  fetch_tfvars(customer)
  fetch_cloud_tags(resource_ids)
  fail_if(mismatch)

Operational rollback matrix (quick mapping)
- Symptom: rising 5xxs within 10m -> action: pause rollout, rollback last batch, revert routing rule change, escalate to SRE.
- Symptom: control-plane DNS failures -> action: switch to alternate control-plane endpoint, rollback tf change that touched route53, notify network owner.
- Symptom: tfstate lock errors across pipeline -> action: abort all applies, manual unlock + revalidate, do not retry automations until human ack.

Edge cases we saw (notes from customer incidents)
- Some colo providers (customer X) run a NAT gateway with /29 allocation; our new sidecar ranges overlapped. Build a small preflight that warns about overlapping /29s.
- Customers with egress proxies that rewrite host headers caused JWT audience mismatches after we introduced proxy sidecars. Add a JWT audience lint to preflight.

Checklist for SEs before scheduling an upgrade
- [ ] Verify tfstate snapshot exists and is accessible to ops (s3/gcs path)
- [ ] Confirm customer network rotation window and point of contact is on the call
- [ ] Run plan-only check and capture the plan JSON
- [ ] Run CIDR overlap preflight (script attached below)
- [ ] Confirm canary host mapping + which traces to follow
- [ ] Backdoor rollback recipe validated (how to revert route + how to re-initialize sidecar)

Quick CIDR overlap preflight (bash one-liner)

  ./scripts/check_cidr_overlap.sh --existing "10.10.0.0/16" --candidate "10.10.128.0/17" || echo "OVERLAP" && exit 1

Open questions / TODOs
- Who owns the automated tfstate copy job? (SRE or SE infra?) -> assign a ticket
- Should we integrate Murphy tests into the upgrade CI? Pros: reproducible. Cons: false positives slow rollouts. Proposal: keep them manual for now, automate after 2 successful customer upgrades.
- Add an option to our TF modules for "sidecar-network-exclusion" to avoid overlapping customer reserved ranges. Need API design review.

Action items (next week)
- Miguel: prototype the tfstate-copy CI step and add plan-output sanitizer (JIRA-PI-4123)
- Sofia: implement the CIDR overlap script and add to onboarding checklist (PR link in linked_artifacts)
- Aisha: draft the SE runbook with step-by-step CLI commands and Slack playbook for midnight rollbacks

Notes to self
- Keep the Murphy tests as short and reversible; the goal is early detection, not exhaustive chaos testing.
- Record a short Loom showing the plan-only workflow for the SEs.

Appendix: quick references
- Slack threads: #private-deploy-upgrades (link in Confluence page)
- Example PR: github.com/redwood-inference/tf-modules/pull/876 (contains the module bump we are testing)
- Related Confluence: confluence.redwood/vpc-upgrades-readme
